partner_context.their_ambition: You are the world's mobility demand layer — one app for rides, and increasingly the front-end for autonomous fleets you don't have to own. Your strategy is platform-over-assets: aggregate demand, partner for supply, and add every viable mode.
partner_context.their_pressure: Land ride-hail is mature in your core markets. Your growth edges are new surfaces (air, water), autonomy, and premium tiers — and rivals are moving on all three.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the water-mobility supply layer for your demand engine: a software-defined, autonomy-ready foiling fleet that plugs into your app exactly like your robotaxi partners do — mode by mode, city by city.

hero.title: Uber × Navier — the water layer of the world's mobility platform
hero.subtitle: Uber aggregates demand and partners for supply. Navier is the foiling water supply — autonomy-ready, app-native.
hero.what_we_do_together: Uber adds a foiling water tier the same way it adds robotaxis: Navier supplies the software-defined fleet and runs the network; Uber supplies the demand, the app, and the rider relationship. We start where Uber is already pushing the frontier — the autonomous-forward Gulf — then extend to coastal metros worldwide.

why_now: You and WeRide are deploying 1,200 robotaxis across Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Riyadh by 2027, in partnership with Dubai's RTA — you've shown you'll put partner-operated autonomous fleets in your app. Navier's software-defined, autonomy-ready foiling vessels are the same model on the water — and a ~100-vessel network is already ramping in the Maldives (WSJ/Bloomberg, 2026).
multimodal_fit: Same playbook as Uber's robotaxi partnerships: partner-operated supply, Uber-owned demand and rider experience. The water leg books door-to-door with an UberX at each pier — one app, one account, a new surface.

objections.concern: Why water for a ride-hail platform?
objections.response: Because Uber's coastal markets — the Gulf, NYC, Miami, the Bay, SE Asia — lose hours to congestion on trips that are minutes by water. It's incremental demand on a surface no competitor has claimed.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time. A step-change in marine mobility, not an incremental faster boat.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the open ocean and the berths and jetties already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all. That's the fundamental contrast with flying taxis and other new-infrastructure modes: nothing to permit, build, or wait for.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the 'no charging at the islands' excuse. Autonomy is arriving on the water before the road. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.

end_state.headline: The on-demand water layer of Uber — US coastal metros and the Caribbean network.
end_state.addressable_footprint: The real-use-case clusters where Uber already owns ground demand and water separates riders from destinations — Miami, Palm Beach, Naples–Fort Myers and Tampa Bay in Florida; the Bahamas, USVI/BVI, Puerto Rico and St-Maarten/St-Barths in the Caribbean; Oʻahu and Maui in Hawaiʻi; and the San Francisco Bay.

steady_state.total_markets: 11 coastal clusters across the US and Caribbean
steady_state.platform_mix: Pioneer II for intra-metro and short island hops; Quanta-LR for Miami↔Bahamas and inter-island Caribbean and Hawaiian legs
steady_state.tam_framing: Uber already owns the ground-demand graph in every one of these metros; the water trips — Miami to the Bahamas, across the Bay, between the Hawaiian islands — are a premium surface no ride-hail has ever booked.

end_state.narrative: Steady state is 'request a boat' inside the Uber app across every US coastal metro and the Caribbean network: the same demand graph Uber already owns, extended onto quiet foiling vessels wherever water is the fastest line between two points.

differentiation_vs_status_quo: Scheduled public ferries are a different product. Navier in your app is on-demand, premium, door-to-door — a ride, not a timetable.
Scheduled public ferries are slow and infrequent; an in-app on-demand foiling tier is a premium ride.
